content: Testing sexual or drug-injecting partners of individuals with HIV, either together or separately, is recommended for key populations. Provider-assisted referral, also known as assisted partner notification or index testing, involves offering voluntary HIV testing services (HTS) to the sexual and drug-injecting partners of people with HIV, including those in key populations. This approach is recommended as part of a comprehensive care package for all individuals with HIV. Testing biological children of key population members with HIV should also be considered as part of provider-assisted referral. This approach must be implemented safely to protect clients from violence or persecution, particularly those from socially marginalized or criminalized key populations. Health services should be provided in a safe environment, free from law enforcement involvement, to enable key populations and other vulnerable groups to access necessary care. Raising community awareness, monitoring potential harms, and modifying programs to address these harms are critical. Social network-based HIV testing approaches can increase testing uptake by targeting the social, sexual, or drug-injecting contacts of both HIV-positive and HIV-negative individuals in key populations. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends offering social network-based approaches as part of partner services for key populations, especially where uptake of provider-assisted referral is low. Integrating HTS with other testing and prevention services, such as screening for sexually transmitted infections (STIs), tuberculosis (TB), and viral hepatitis, can enhance benefits. Community-based HTS offering multi-disease testing, including HIV and STI testing, has shown high uptake and effective case finding among key populations. HTS also provides an opportunity to deliver prevention services, such as condom distribution, reproductive health services, needle-syringe programs, and opioid substitution therapy. WHO recommends social network-based HIV testing as part of a comprehensive care and prevention package for key populations. HIV self-testing (HIVST) is also recommended as an effective approach to HTS. Trained lay providers can independently conduct safe and effective HIV testing using rapid diagnostic tests. Voluntary HIV testing should be routinely offered to all clients from key populations in clinical settings, including those for STIs, viral hepatitis, TB, immunization, malnutrition, and antenatal care (ANC). Community-based HTS, linked to prevention, treatment, and care, should complement facility-based testing for key populations. Globally, men with HIV are less likely than women to know their status, be on treatment, or achieve viral suppression. In 2018, only 55% of adult men with HIV were receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART), compared to 68% of women. This disparity is most pronounced in sub-Saharan Africa, where fewer men than women with HIV are aware of their status or on treatment. Consequently, HIV-related morbidity and mortality rates are higher among men. Men from key populations bear a significant HIV burden, with many remaining undiagnosed. Outside Africa, men from key populations account for more new HIV infections than women. These gaps hinder global efforts to achieve HIV testing, treatment, and prevention targets. Men’s lower uptake of health services is attributed to structural and behavioral barriers, including stigma, fear, and the perception that health services are designed primarily for women and children. Differentiated HTS approaches, combining facility-based and community-based strategies, are essential for reaching men. Strategic service delivery approaches should consider men’s preferences, local context, epidemiology, and available resources. In high HIV burden settings, such as southern Africa, efforts should target men from both general and key populations. In low HIV burden settings, approaches should focus on men from key populations, including clients of sex workers, men with STIs or TB, and men with HIV-positive partners who are not on ART or virally suppressed. Across all HTS approaches, men diagnosed with HIV require support to link to ART promptly. Men should also be engaged in HIV prevention interventions, such as voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) services, and tested at least annually if HIV-negative and in serodiscordant relationships. Men taking PrEP require quarterly HTS integrated with STI and viral hepatitis screening. Facility-based HTS remains an important access point for men, often when they are ill and in advanced stages of HIV disease. Routine HTS should be offered to men in high HIV burden settings. Community-based HTS is crucial for reaching men, particularly those less likely to use health facilities. Community-based approaches, such as mobile outreach and HIVST distribution, are effective for reaching men who have never tested or are from key populations. Workplace HTS initiatives have identified many previously undiagnosed infections, particularly among men. For example, in South Africa, HIVST implementation in a mining company led to significant uptake, with 42% of participants having never tested or not tested in the past year. Workplace HTS should be implemented within policies that protect workers from discrimination and job loss. Adolescents and young people, particularly those aged 10–24 years, are highly vulnerable to HIV due to social, cultural, and economic factors. However, they are less likely to be tested than adults, leaving many undiagnosed and untreated. Adolescents from key populations face even greater challenges in accessing HTS. HTS should be prioritized for perinatally infected adolescents, key population adolescents, and those at high risk, such as street children, orphans, and sexually exploited youth. In high HIV burden settings, HTS should be routinely offered to adolescents and young people. Community-based outreach and HIVST can improve access to HTS for this group. HIVST has been shown to double HTS uptake among adolescents and young people compared to standard facility-based testing. HTS for adolescents should be adolescent-friendly, addressing their psychological and physical health needs in a confidential, non-judgmental, and non-stigmatizing manner. Referral and linkage pathways to prevention, treatment, and care services are crucial. Social media and web-based campaigns can reduce barriers to HTS access. Adolescents taking PrEP should receive quarterly HTS integrated with STI screening.
